sections.markdown:
## C2 — Confusable pairs and knowledge-graph hints: hand signals, hill parking, the two one-hundred-foot figures, stopping table rows and parking steps
Confusable pairs among steering, signal, reversing and parking rules, followed by continuation facts and step-by-step maneuver details the C block left out for size; each block ties to one handbook page, and hint metadata sits only in the trailing line of a block.

FACT_ID: sec05-R01 | anchor: A04
The three driver hand signals are easy to mix up: arm down with the palm to the rear means stop or slow, arm up means a right turn, and arm straight out means a left turn. [A04]
Why it matters: group signals; confusable stop versus right versus left.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec05-R02 | anchor: A04
Bicyclists, skateboarders and inline skaters use the same hand signals, but may also signal a right turn by holding the right arm straight out. [A04]
Why it matters: group signals; confusable driver versus cyclist right-turn signal.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec05-R03 | anchor: A07
Downhill against a curb the wheels turn toward the curb and a manual gearbox goes in reverse, while uphill against a curb the wheels turn away from the curb and a manual gearbox goes in low. [A07]
Why it matters: group parking; confusable downhill versus uphill.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec05-R04 | anchor: A05
Two different figures of about 100 feet are easy to confuse: the road test asks you to back up about 100 feet in a straight line, and state law requires moving into the proper lane and signaling at least 100 feet before any turn. [A05]
Why it matters: group distances; confusable reversing distance versus signal distance.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec05-R05 | anchor: A05
While reversing, the front of the vehicle swings in the opposite direction from the turn. [A05]
Why it matters: group reversing; misconception front follows the turn.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec05-R06 | anchor: A05
Plan turns well ahead, since last-minute turns can be unsafe, and the faster traffic is moving the earlier the turn should be planned. [A05]
Why it matters: group turning; difficulty low.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec05-R07 | anchor: A04
Before backing up, make sure the path is clear by using the mirrors and also turning to look, because the view to the rear is limited. [A04]
Why it matters: group reversing; difficulty low.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec05-R08 | anchor: A01
Hand-over-hand steering covers adjustments from very small up to about half a turn of the wheel while both hands stay on it; in a gentle curve the hands usually keep their grip and make only slight finger or wrist movements. [A01]
Why it matters: group steering; difficulty medium.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec05-R09 | anchor: A01
Grip the wheel firmly but not too tightly, and hold it as steady as possible as speed increases. [A01]
Why it matters: group steering; difficulty low.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec05-R10 | anchor: A02
A hand-over-hand turn starts by pushing the wheel up from the 9 or 3 o'clock position toward 12 while the other hand crosses over and down, after which the first hand returns to its starting position. [A02]
Why it matters: group steering; difficulty high.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec05-R11 | anchor: A02
To straighten after a turn, reverse the hand movements or let the wheel slide through the fingers (controlled slipping) while both hands stay on the wheel. [A02]
Why it matters: group steering; difficulty medium.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec05-R12 | anchor: A02
There is no simple way to know exactly how long a vehicle will take to stop at a given speed. [A02]
Why it matters: group stopping; misconception a fixed stopping distance.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec05-R13 | anchor: A03
The manual's stopping table gives a total of 102 feet at 30 mph, made up of 33 feet of reaction distance and 69 feet of braking distance. [A03]
Why it matters: group stopping; difficulty medium.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec05-R14 | anchor: A03
The manual's stopping table gives a total of 343 feet at 60 mph, made up of 66 feet of reaction distance and 277 feet of braking distance. [A03]
Why it matters: group stopping; difficulty medium.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec05-R15 | anchor: A03
The manual's stopping table gives a total of 453 feet at 70 mph, made up of 77 feet of reaction distance and 376 feet of braking distance. [A03]
Why it matters: group stopping; difficulty high.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec05-R16 | anchor: A03
The manual's stopping table gives a total of 19 feet at 10 mph, made up of 11 feet of reaction distance and 8 feet of braking distance. [A03]
Why it matters: group stopping; difficulty medium.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec05-R17 | anchor: A03
The manual puts typical deceleration at approximately 14 feet per second. [A03]
Why it matters: group stopping; difficulty high.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec05-R18 | anchor: A03
Whether a vehicle has front-wheel or rear-wheel drive does not decide how to brake; what matters is knowing whether it has conventional drum and disc brakes or ABS. [A03]
Why it matters: group braking; misconception drive type sets braking.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec05-R19 | anchor: A03
Until they get used to ABS, new drivers are advised to rehearse hard stops and steering in an empty lot or another open space. [A03]
Why it matters: group braking; difficulty low.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec05-R20 | anchor: A06
Slow down before reaching the intersection, then keep a steady speed and follow the pavement markings through the turn. [A06]
Why it matters: group turning; difficulty low.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec05-R21 | anchor: A07
To enter an angle space on your right, watch traffic ahead and behind, signal and slow, make sure your rear end will clear the parked cars, steer sharply in, then straighten the wheels to center the vehicle and shift to park with the parking brake on. [A07]
Why it matters: group parking; difficulty medium.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec05-R22 | anchor: A07
Before backing out of an angle space, walk around the vehicle to make sure nothing is in its way, then reverse slowly while making sure the lane is clear. [A07]
Why it matters: group parking; difficulty low.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec05-R23 | anchor: A08
When backing out of an angle space, keep turning slowly until the left front wheel passes the rear bumper of the car parked on the left, then straighten the wheels as you re-enter the traffic lane. [A08]
Why it matters: group parking; difficulty medium.
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec05-R24 | anchor: A08
Before backing into a parallel space, signal for a stop and signal right to show that you will back up to the right, then turn to check that the way behind is clear. [A08]
Why it matters: group parallel parking; difficulty low.
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec05-R25 | anchor: A08
Looking out the rear window, back up slowly for about two feet and then turn the steering wheel fully to the right. [A08]
Why it matters: group parallel parking; difficulty medium.
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec05-R26 | anchor: A08
When the front of your vehicle clears the rear bumper of the car ahead, stop, check the angle and make sure the right rear wheel has not struck the curb. [A08]
Why it matters: group parallel parking; difficulty medium.
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec05-R27 | anchor: A08
Next turn the wheel fully to the left while backing slowly, stop once the vehicle is in line without touching the car behind, then straighten the wheels and pull to the center of the space. [A08]
Why it matters: group parallel parking; difficulty medium.
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec05-R28 | anchor: A08
The slower and smoother you back into a parking space, the easier parking becomes. [A08]
Why it matters: group parallel parking; difficulty low.
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0060]
